newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PacDun sees US glove buy earnings positive.
newsitem.headline: PacDun sees US glove buy earnings positive.

text.p: Australian-based industrial group Pacific Dunlop Ltd planned to finance its A$115 million purchase of U.S. safety glove maker Golden Needles Knitting Inc (GKN) from internal resources, managing director Rod Chadwick said on Monday.
Chadwick also said the purchase would be earnings positive immediately and would raise Pacific Dunlop's share of the U.S. industrial glove market to about 40 percent from 35 percent.
"It's earnings positive from today," Chadwick told Reuters.
Pacific Dunlop's Ansell International unit saw the GNK purchase providing synergies and strengthening its position in Europe as well.
"It broadens out the Ansell product range within the industrial glove market," Chadwick said.
He said GNK's four factories in North Carolina were well established and did not need any great investment immediately and they might even be room to cut some costs.
"There might be some rationalisation," he said.
GNK has annual sales of A$120 million and has 1,700 automated glove knitting machines.

The acquisition would add to Ansell's worldwide sales, which last year totalled A$825 million, comprising 400 million pairs of industrial gloves, 350 million pairs of surgeons gloves, 2.5 billion medical examination gloves and 450 million condoms.
Chadwick said the GNK acquisition was not an indication of a new spending spree, although Pacific Dunlop continued to look at opportunities in identified growth sectors.
He said Pacific Dunlop would look at similar sized acquisitions rather than anything larger or smaller.
"We think acquisitions of this size of about A$100 million are the right size to grow the business," Chadwick said.
He would not say which sectors Pacific Dunlop had identified, although he noted that Ansell would now take some time to absorb the GNK business.
"This will keep them busy for a period," he said.
Pacific Dunlop continued to examine its six main businesses to see they were above target weighted average cost of capital ratios, Chadwick said.
He said Pacific Dunlop's battery division was not meeting its targets, but that the group saw the potential for a significant turnaround.
Chadwick said there was a possibility that Pacific Dunlop could divest one of its six businesses, but that he could not say which of the six were more vulnerable to divestment.
Pacific Dunlop closed two cents lower at A$3.42 on Monday.
